question: Which original studies compare competing against a believed-human opponent with a known-computer opponent in competitive games, with enjoyment-related outcomes?

claims.text: [1] population: players of a tank shooter in fMRI
fragments: Participants played a competitive tank shooter game against alleged human and computer opponents while their brain activity was measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging.

claims.text: [1] exposure: alleged human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer opponent
fragments: Participants played a competitive tank shooter game against alleged human and computer opponents while their brain activity was measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging.

claims.text: [1] results: ventral striatum tracked self-rated pleasure; vmPFC and dorsal striatum responded more to winning against a human; design fMRI
fragments: Activation in ventral striatum was associated with participants' self-ratings of pleasure.
The vmPFC and dorsal striatum responses were stronger to winning when the subject was playing against a human rather than a computer.

elements.card: vmPFC and dorsal striatum stronger for human

claims.text: [2] population: players of a video game; exposure: computer, friend or stranger as opponent; comparator: computer; design: self-report, interbeat intervals, facial EMG
fragments: In addition to self-report ratings, cardiac interbeat intervals (IBIs) and facial electromyography (EMG) were measured to index physiological arousal and emotional valence.

claims.text: [2] results: more presence, engagement and positive emotion against humans; abstract does not state whether participants were deceived
fragments: playing against another human elicited higher spatial presence, engagement, anticipated threat, post-game challenge appraisals, and physiological arousal, as well as more positively valenced emotional responses.

elements.card: more presence, engagement, positive emotion vs humans

claims.text: [3] population: players of a video game with non co-located opponents; exposure: human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer
fragments: participants played Super Monkey Ball Jr. and Duke Nukem Advance against a computer, a non co-located friend, and a non co-located stranger.

claims.text: [3] results: more positive emotion, arousal, presence and engagement against a human; design: EMG, interbeat intervals, skin conductance
fragments: playing against a human elicited more positive emotional responses and higher arousal, spatial presence, and engagement.

elements.card: more positive emotion, arousal, presence, engagement vs human

claims.text: [4] population: twenty Call of Duty players; exposure: same agent told to be agent or avatar; comparator: opponent told to be an agent
fragments: Although participants played against an agent in both matches, participants were told that they were playing against an agent in one match, and an avatar in the other.

elements.source: Twenty participants played Call of Duty

elements.card: same agent told agent or avatar

claims.text: [4] results: arousal differences when the enemy was first met, mixed measures later, some players not convinced of humanity
fragments: Significant differences in participants' arousal level were found when the enemy was first encountered, though measures became more mixed as the interactions played out.

elements.card: arousal differences at first encounter, mixed later, not all convinced

claims.text: [5] population: participants in rock-paper-scissors fMRI; exposure: believed human, humanoid robot or random computer; comparator: random computer
fragments: Participants were scanned using fMRI during interactive rock-paper-scissors games while believing their opponent was a fellow human (Intentional agent, Int)

elements.card: believed human, humanoid robot, random computer

claims.text: [5] results: activity human > robot > random; mPFC and right TPJ responded to the human only; design fMRI
fragments: brain activity for Art was larger than for Rnd but lower than for Int, supporting the intrinsically engaging nature of social interactions.
mentalizing regions, the medial prefrontal cortex and right temporoparietal junction, responded to the human only

elements.card: human > robot > random; mPFC and rTPJ human only

claims.text: [6] population: participants in three experiments (N = 74, 788 and 500); exposure: competing against an AI or a believed human in a logical-thinking task; comparator: believed human
fragments: Experiments 1 ( N  = 74) and 2 ( N  = 788) recruited Japanese participants, while Experiment 3 ( N  = 500) comprised American participants.

claims.text: [6] results: re-challenge did not differ in two experiments and was lower in the AI condition in one
fragments: The number of participants choosing to re-challenge the game did not differ significantly between the AI and human conditions in Experiments 1 and 3, although the number was lower in the AI condition than in the human condition in Experiment 2.

elements.card: no difference in two, lower for AI in one

claims.text: [9] population: players of online games; exposure: computer- vs human-controlled opponent; comparator: computer-controlled
[9] results and design: not available, only the title (presence, flow and enjoyment) was read
[13] population: volunteers in stone-paper-scissors PET; exposure: believed to play the experimenter or a computer; comparator: computer
fragments: In the mentalizing condition volunteers believed they were playing against the experimenter. In the comparison condition, volunteers believed they were playing against a computer.

claims.text: [13] results: only anterior paracingulate cortex more active under the intentional stance; design PET; no enjoyment measure
fragments: Only one region was more active when volunteers adopted the intentional stance. This was in anterior paracingulate cortex (bilaterally).

claims.text: [14] population: participants in a competitive gain-loss game; exposure: human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer
fragments: simultaneously with motivational processes of gains and losses in playing against a human or a computer opponent.

elements.card: competitive gain-loss game, human vs computer

claims.text: [14] results: network sensitive to opponent type (human > computer); design: two fMRI studies
fragments: We report the results of two fMRI studies using a competitive game
opponent type (human>computer)

claims.text: [15] population: participants in matching pennies; exposure: told human or computer with the same algorithm; comparator: computer
fragments: subjects played matching pennies with either a human or computer opponent in each block, although in reality they played the game with the same computer algorithm under both conditions.

elements.card: told human or computer, same algorithm

claims.text: [15] results: opponent affected behavioural entropy; anterior insula tracked entropy; design fMRI
fragments: Both the opponent (human or computer), and the winning rate, independently affected subjects' block-wise entropy during the game.

elements.card: opponent affected entropy; insula tracked entropy

claims.text: [16] population: participants in a card-guessing game; exposure: close friend, confederate or random number generator; comparator: random number generator
fragments: a close friend (in-network), a confederate (out-of-network) and a random number generator (non-social condition)

claims.text: [16] results: striatal responses stronger for social than non-social competitors in an exploratory analysis; design fMRI
fragments: which an exploratory analysis revealed to be stronger when interacting with social, compared with non-social, competitors.

claims.text: [17] population: participants in an iterated prisoner's dilemma; exposure: computer, functional robot, anthropomorphic robot or human partner; comparator: computer partner
fragments: Increasing degrees of human-likeness for the game partner were introduced by means of a computer partner, a functional robot, an anthropomorphic robot and a human partner.

elements.card: IPD; computer, functional robot, anthropomorphic robot, human

claims.text: [17] results: more fun and competition with human-likeness; medial frontal and right TPJ activity rose; design fMRI
fragments: participants indicated having experienced more fun and competition in the interaction with increasing human-like features of their partners.

elements.card: more fun and competition; MFC and rTPJ rose

claims.text: [19] population: participants in matching pennies; exposure: human, android, robots or computer; comparator: computer
fragments: simple matching-pennies game with a human, human-like android, mechanical robot, interactive robot, and a computer.

elements.card: matching pennies; human, android, robots, computer

claims.text: [19] results: impressions of agents modulated dorsal and ventral pathway activity; design fMRI
fragments: different impressions obtained through social interaction with a variety of agents uniquely modulate activity of dorsal and ventral pathways

elements.card: impressions modulated dorsal and ventral pathways

claims.text: [7] population: 30 unimpaired and 8 stroke participants; exposure: competitive (human) air-hockey mode; comparator: single-player against the computer
fragments: single-player (competing against computer), competitive (competing against human)
All modes were played by 30 unimpaired subjects and 8 impaired chronic stroke subjects.

claims.text: [7] results: unimpaired participants preferred two-player modes; those liking competition put in more effort; Intrinsic Motivation Inventory
fragments: Nearly all unimpaired subjects preferred playing the two-player game modes to the single-player one
Unimpaired subjects who liked the competitive mode also put significantly more effort into it than into the other modes.

elements.card: preferred two-player; competition-likers more effort; IMI

claims.text: [8] population: rehabilitation participants over several sessions; exposure: three sessions against a human then one against a computer; comparator: computer
fragments: All participants first played the game against their human opponent for 3 sessions, then played alone (against a computer opponent) in the final, fourth session.

claims.text: [8] results: friend or relative at home showed higher enjoyment and exercise intensity; clinic pairs no significant difference
fragments: exhibited higher enjoyment and exercise intensity when competing (first three sessions) than when exercising alone (last session).
Participants who played against each other in the clinic, however, did not exhibit significant differences between competition and exercising alone.

claims.text: [20] population: participants in an online image-recognition game; exposure: told computer- or human-controlled opponent (always computer); comparator: presumed human
fragments: Participants were told that they would play an online image recognition game against a computer- or a human-controlled opponent. In both cases, participants faced a computer-controlled opponent

claims.text: [20] results: copresence higher against a computer-controlled opponent in one condition; outcome is social presence
fragments: The sense of copresence was even higher when they were facing a computer-controlled opponent rather than a presumed human-controlled one.

elements.card: copresence higher vs computer-controlled; social presence outcome

claims.text: [10] population: Wii Boxing players; exposure: human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer
fragments: The subjects were randomised to play against a human or computer opponent while heart rate, oxygen consumption and energy expenditure were measured.

claims.text: [10] results: no difference in heart rate or oxygen consumption
fragments: No significant differences were found in heart rates whencomparing the two video game opponents or the males and females.

claims.text: [12] population: female game players; exposure: human vs computer opponent; comparator: computer
fragments: Studies 2 and 3 indicate that playing against a human opponent (rather than a computer) increases aggressive thoughts.

claims.text: [12] results: human opponent increased aggressive thoughts; presence the other outcome
fragments: Studies 2 and 3 indicate that playing against a human opponent (rather than a computer) increases aggressive thoughts.

elements.card: human increased aggressive thoughts; presence other outcome

elements.card: human vs computer partner, resource conflicts

claims.text: [18] results: more sharing with a human partner; design fMRI
fragments: Behaviorally, participants shared much more often when playing with a human partner than with a computer.
